body:
# Independent audit: equality in the effective cap-count profile



Source: `candidate 8b5860c585f8735a`.

**Result: PASS**, using the stated strict inverse-power radial-rigidity
theorem as an explicit dependency. I read both the classification source
and `candidate 07f233a26b321ff2`, and checked
the latter's interface here independently. Coherent is independently
auditing that dependency's full radial equality proof. I also use the
already audited hereditary profile and strict open-cover results; our
separate audit of the latter is
`historical context (not an accepted premise)`.

## 1. The strict exponent and support conditions are preserved

Every full-dimensional integrable log-concave density belongs to the
inverse-power class for every beta>0. In the application one may fix,
for example, beta=r+2, which is strictly larger than r+1. Restricting
the density to the retained closed convex set preserves log-concavity.
Its positive-mass restriction has full-dimensional convex positive
interior; boundary values may be removed on a Lebesgue-null set.
Thus the dependency is used in the strict exponent range and in
dimension r>=2, exactly as required. No equality theorem for the
borderline projective exponent beta=r+1 is assumed.

The dependency supplies an attained deepest point in the positive
interior and an a.e. simplex-gauge representation. Its profile is
positive on [0,R), nonincreasing and log-concave there, with support
closure either the entire space or a positive homothetic simplex.
Here and in the theorem statement, finite radial integral means
the mass condition integral_0^R t^(r-1) F(t)dt<infinity, with positive
value. This is the normalization actually used by polar integration.

## 2. Distal equality really forces minimal maximal depth

Under positive-part equality the nominal retained mass is
alpha/Gamma_r>0. Distal trimming loses at most the sum of prescribed
outer-piece masses. Every original cap has restricted mass at most
alpha, and those caps still cover the retained support. Therefore
hereditary depth gives an upper bound alpha/Gamma_r on the retained
mass, which matches its lower bound. The cap cover also bounds every
candidate's normalized depth by Gamma_r. Hereditary depth gives the
opposite bound at an attained point, so the retained density has
maximal depth exactly Gamma_r.

Equality in the removed-piece union bound is justified for the actual
density measure, not just Lebesgue volume: integrate the finite sum of
indicators minus their union indicator. Every pairwise overlap has
zero density mass. The positive density on its interior will later
convert any open overlap there into a contradiction.

The retained density therefore satisfies the complete ordinary
minimal-depth classification in the stated dependency. No mixed
measure, noninteger center, or ambient lattice transformation is
substituted into this step.

## 3. All original cap planes and orientations are recovered

At the retained deepest point y, an original cap containing y has
restricted mass at most alpha and at least alpha. If it contained y
strictly, moving its parallel plane to y would remove a positive
local slab: the density has a positive lower bound on a sufficiently
small closed ball about y in its positive support. This contradicts
the through-y lower bound. Thus every such cap has boundary through
y and mass alpha.

Polar integration for a simplex-gauge profile preserves the fraction
of every through-y halfspace. Hence this cap cuts the uniform gauge
simplex with fraction Gamma_r. The ordinary equality characterization
identifies its actual plane and orientation as a canonical vertex
cap. Its plane is uniquely determined because the reference simplex
is full-dimensional and the equality plane cuts its interior.

The finitely many caps missing y miss a common neighborhood of y.
The remaining canonical caps must cover that neighborhood. Any proper
subset of the r+1 canonical normals is linearly independent: they
are positive multiples of a proper subset of the simplex barycentric
gradients, and any r of those gradients are independent. Solve their
scalar products equal to -1 to produce a direction excluded by every
cap of the subset. A small displacement of y in this direction stays
in the positive support, contradicting local coverage. Therefore all
r+1 original caps are the distinct canonical through-y caps.

## 4. Positive removal creates a forbidden facet

If A_i>alpha, the removed amount A_i-alpha is positive and the retained
band has positive mass alpha. Therefore its retaining threshold t_i
strictly exceeds the original threshold b_i=ell_i(y). At y all other
actual retaining inequalities are strict as well.

A positive removed density mass yields a point in the positive support
interior and strictly beyond this cut, avoiding all the other finitely
many cutting planes. This point cannot be strictly beyond another cut:
an open intersection inside the positive support would have positive
density mass, violating the equality in the union bound. Thus it
strictly satisfies all other retained inequalities.

The segment to y crosses the chosen retaining plane inside the original
positive support and strictly inside every other retained side. A
small neighborhood of the crossing contains a relatively open
(r-1)-disk in the support boundary of the retained density. It is a
genuine supporting facet patch, not merely an a.e. trace assertion.

For a gauge profile with R=infinity, the support closure is all R^r.
The finite retaining cut bounds a ray from y and contradicts that
possibility. For R finite and positive the support closure is a
homothetic simplex. The recovered canonical cap normal exposes exactly
its associated vertex, and cannot expose an (r-1)-dimensional patch
when r>=2. This excludes positive trimming in both possible support
regimes. Hence the original and retained densities agree a.e., and
all masses equal alpha=Gamma_r V.

Conversely, a log-concave nonincreasing simplex-gauge profile has the
same angular cap fractions as its reference simplex. Its canonical
through-center caps cover the entire space and each has fraction
Gamma_r. This proves the claimed sufficiency exactly, with arbitrary
finite or infinite radial support satisfying the stated mass condition.

## 5. Ordinary D-dimensional few-cap corollary

For 3<=m<=D+1 put r=m-1. A proper subcover has j<m and effective
dimension j-1<r. Its profile, the nonnegative omitted summands and
the strict inequality Gamma_(j-1)>Gamma_r make the original profile
strict for alpha>0. A one-cap subcover uses Gamma_0=1. Thus equality
requires minimality.

If the original normal rank rho is below r, ordinary projection gives
a full-dimensional log-concave marginal in dimension rho, preserving
all masses. Its hereditary constant Gamma_rho is strictly larger,
again excluding equality. If the rank is m, necessarily m<=D and
the already audited independent-normal theorem applies. Its
projective affine margin sum is 1 and hence gives an open cover,
making the profile strict without any borderline density rigidity
assumption. The only remaining normal rank is r.

Projection onto that rank-r span preserves the original cap family
and total mass, and produces the log-concave marginal to which the
first theorem applies. This proves all three stated necessary
conditions. Their sufficiency follows from the same angular mass
identity. In the endpoint case m=D+1 the projection is full-dimensional
and the marginal is uniform volume itself, recovering the previously
audited ordinary simplex/canonical-cap theorem.

The source correctly makes no statement for m>D+1 and no uniform
stability statement as independent normals approach dependence.
Every transformation in the proof is an ordinary continuous
projection or normalization. No mixed-integer load comparison or OC
conclusion follows from this classification alone.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
